text: AWS Secrets Manager is purpose-built for storing secrets like database credentials, API keys, and OAuth tokens, and its defining feature is automatic rotation. For supported services -- most notably Amazon RDS -- it can rotate the stored credential on a schedule with no manual intervention: generating a new password, updating it on the RDS instance, and updating the stored value, all through a managed rotation Lambda function AWS provides.

An application that always fetches the current value from Secrets Manager at connection time never notices the password changed underneath it. That reliability is what you're paying for -- Secrets Manager charges per secret stored per month, plus per API call, which is the cost side of the tradeoff this lesson is building toward.

Systems Manager Parameter Store stores configuration values and secrets as named, hierarchical parameters, like /prod/orders-service/db-host. Its Standard tier is free for a generous number of parameters and calls, which makes it the default for ordinary configuration -- feature flags, hostnames, non-sensitive settings. It also supports basic secrets as an encrypted SecureString type, but it has no built-in rotation workflow -- rotating one yourself is something you'd script.

So the decision isn't which service is better -- it's which property a given value needs most. A production database password that must be rotated on a schedule is worth Secrets Manager's cost. A feature flag or an internal hostname doesn't need rotation at all, so paying Secrets Manager's per-secret charge for it would be wasted spend. Parameter Store covers that case for free.

That cost-versus-rotation tradeoff is the real reason AWS offers two overlapping services instead of one. Next: what rotation actually buys you when a credential does leak, and the least-privilege access-policy practice that limits who can read a secret in the first place.
